summary: Defines a new Proxy Mobile IPv6 mobility option, the IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector, which lets the local mobility anchor and the mobile access gateway negotiate which IPv4 traffic flows may be offloaded directly instead of via the core.

eli5.summary: Some of your mail can take a shortcut near home instead of the long route to head office. This option lets both sides agree on which mail.

subtitle: A Proxy Mobile IPv6 option that lets two nodes agree which IPv4 flows skip the tunnel home and leave at the access network.

tldr.problem: In Proxy Mobile IPv6 all of a mobile node's traffic is tunneled from the access network back to the home network, with no way to send some flows out locally.
tldr.mechanism: A new mobility option, the IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector (53), rides in the Proxy Binding Update and Acknowledgement and carries traffic selectors plus a mode flag saying which flows to offload.
tldr.outcome: A mobile access gateway can send selected IPv4 flows straight out of the access network and tunnel the rest. IPv6 flows are not covered.

today: RFC 6909 is a Proposed Standard published in April 2013. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem: Everything Goes Home
sections.content:
Mobile operators are combining several access technologies (such as Wireless LAN, CDMA and LTE) into a common IP mobility core. In the 3GPP S2a Proxy Mobile IPv6 design, the mobile node's IP traffic is always tunneled from the mobile access gateway (MAG) in the access network to the local mobility anchor (LMA) in the home network. There was no mechanism to let some flows be offloaded in the access network.

With the growth in mobile data traffic, operators want to offload some flows at the nearest access edge, either for local service access or for Internet offload. Traffic that does not need IP mobility support need not go home, which allows efficient use of the mobile packet core and helps lower transport costs. How to classify traffic is up to the operator: one might offload everything except traffic such as Voice over IP that needs QoS, another might offload only HTTP.

The RFC notes one limitation: IPsec-encrypted traffic with no visibility into the application payload cannot be selected for offload.
sections.eli5: Right now every parcel you send has to go to head office first. Some parcels could just be dropped at the local post office, which is cheaper.

sections.title: How the Offload Fits Together
sections.content:
The RFC defines a new option for Proxy Mobile IPv6 that the LMA and MAG use to negotiate an IPv4 traffic offload policy for a mobility session. The policy lists the flow selectors that pick out the flows to offload. An IP flow is a set of packets matching a traffic selector, typically based on source and destination address, ports and other upper-layer header fields.

Because the mobile node's IP address belongs topologically to the home network, offloaded IPv4 flows may need NAT. These flows lose mobility support, since the NAT becomes their anchor point. For local service access, NAT may not be needed if the MAG is in the path of the return traffic. The RFC does not restrict where the NAT sits: it can be on the MAG or at the edge of the access network. Applying NAT depends on local configuration on the MAG.

The scope is IPv4 only. The RFC says there are better ways to address offload for IPv6 and it does not want to create a NAT66 requirement.
sections.eli5: Parcels that take the local shortcut get a new return label, so they cannot follow you if you move. That is the price of the shortcut.

sections.title: The IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector Option
sections.content:
The new mobility option has Type 53 and is used in Proxy Binding Update (PBU) and Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (PBA) messages. Its alignment requirement is 4n. Fields: an 8-bit Type, an 8-bit Length (octets of the option, excluding Type and Length), the M flag, a Reserved field that MUST be set to 0 by the sender and ignored by the receiver, and an optional Traffic Selector sub-option.

The Offload Mode (M) flag sets how the selectors are read. With M=0, flows that match the selectors are offloaded at the MAG and all other flows are tunneled to the LMA. With M=1, all flows except those matching the selectors are offloaded, and the matching flows are tunneled back to the LMA.

The sub-option is optional in a PBU but mandatory in a PBA. Its format comes from Section 4.2.1.4 of RFC 6089, and its TS Format value 1 means the IPv4 binary traffic selector of RFC 6088, which is mandatory to support here. Value 2 (IPv6 binary selector) is not used. Where this text differs from RFC 6088 and RFC 6089, this text takes precedence.
sections.eli5: The option is a little note with a switch. One position says 'send these parcels locally'. The other says 'send everything locally except these'.

sections.title: What the MAG and LMA Do
sections.content:
MAG. If offload is enabled, the MAG includes the option in its PBU. It may leave out the sub-option, which asks the LMA to provide the policy (and the M flag MUST then be 0), or it may include selectors as a proposal. The LMA can accept the proposal or override it. In PBUs for lifetime extension or de-registration, the MAG SHOULD copy the option from the initial PBU. If the MAG does not support offload but receives the option in a PBA, it MUST ignore it. If the PBA has no option, the MAG SHOULD NOT enable offload for that session. If the PBA has the option, the MAG SHOULD enable offload and set up its data plane from the selectors.

LMA. If the PBU lacks the option, the LMA MUST NOT enable offload and the PBA MUST NOT contain the option. If the LMA does not support offload it ignores the option. If it does support it, the LMA MUST enable offload and the PBA MUST include the option. The LMA can get the policy from local configuration or from a network function such as AAA or PCRF.

The selectors MUST match only that mobile node's application traffic. Control-plane traffic such as DHCP, Neighbor Discovery or any traffic used for address configuration or mobility management MUST NOT be offloaded.

The LMA MUST NOT change a mobile node's offload policy mid-session while the node stays attached to the MAG that negotiated it. After an inter-MAG handover the new MAG may not support offload, so the policy may change.
sections.eli5: The local office asks head office 'can I send some parcels locally?' Head office either agrees with the list or writes its own. Important office mail never takes the shortcut.

sections.title: The Configuration Variable
sections.content:
The RFC defines one configuration variable, EnableIPv4TrafficOffloadSupport, on both the MAG and the LMA. It defaults to 0, meaning offload is disabled. On the MAG, setting it to 1 makes the MAG request the offload policy for all mobility sessions by including the option in the PBU. On the LMA, setting it to 1 means that when a policy exists for a mobile node, the LMA delivers it in the PBA.

The variable is internal and has no bearing on interoperability. Configured values have to survive server reboots and service restarts.
sections.eli5: There is an on/off switch, and it starts switched off.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The option is carried like any other mobility header option under RFC 5213, so it inherits that security guidance and does not require any additional considerations. The RFC states that carrying offload selectors does not introduce new security vulnerabilities.

Offloaded flows are typically NAT translated, bringing the vulnerabilities common to any NAT deployment (documented in RFC 2663). Offload also potentially exposes the mobile node to security risks in the access network, which can be mitigated by deploying security features in both the access and home networks. Finally, because some flows go through the home network and others through the access network, diagnostics and monitoring tools have to be aware of the offload policy.
sections.eli5: Taking the shortcut means the parcels skip head office's guards, so the local office needs good guards too.

sections.title: IANA Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned the new mobility option, the IPv4 Traffic Offload Selector option, the value 53, from the same numbering space as the other mobility options defined in RFC 6275.
sections.eli5: The option got its own official number, 53, like a house number.

messages.label: Proxy Binding Update (IPv4TS)
messages.note: Asks for, or proposes, an offload policy.

messages.label: Proxy Binding Acknowledgement (IPv4TS)
messages.note: Carries the policy the MAG should enforce.

messages.label: IPv4 packet from mobile node
messages.note: The MAG applies the offload rule: tunnel or offload.

items.label: Offload the matches
items.desc: Flows matching the selectors are offloaded at the MAG; all other flows are tunneled to the LMA.

items.label: Offload all but the matches
items.desc: Flows matching the selectors are tunneled to the LMA; all other flows are offloaded at the MAG.
